First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-4{y}^{′}+8y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8=0\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{c}(x) & ={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x).\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $20{e}^{2x}.$ In this case, the constant factor in the exponent is $2,$ which is not the root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha {e}^{2x},\,\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=4\alpha {e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute ${y}_{p},$ ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and ${y}_{p}^{″}$ into the ODE and solve for $\alpha :$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\alpha {e}^{2x}-4(2\alpha {e}^{2x})+8(\alpha {e}^{2x}) & =20{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha (4-8+8){e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha {e}^{2x} & =20{e}^{2x} \\ 4\alpha  & =20 \\ \alpha  & =5\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=5{e}^{2x}.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+5{e}^{2x}.
$$

Now let's find the constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=1$ into the general solution gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=2.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=2{e}^{2x}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+{e}^{2x}(-2P\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2Q\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+10{e}^{2x}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=2$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}2P+2Q+10 & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $P=-4$ and $Q=0.$

We substitute this into the general particular integral and find that the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={e}^{2x}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+0)+5{e}^{2x} \\  & =-4{e}^{2x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+5{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$
